items.question: How did you handle offline maps in TrailMate?

answers.why: Concrete mechanism, storage limit decision, edge case handled.
answers.answer: Before a hike you pick the area on the map and the app downloads the tiles for that bounding box at zoom levels 10 to 16 into a local SQLite tile cache. I capped a region at about 150 MB because higher zoom levels grow fast, roughly four times more tiles per level. GPS still works without signal since it doesn't need data, so the track is drawn over the cached tiles, and anything recorded offline syncs to Firebase when the phone reconnects.
Users download the tiles for a selected region and zoom range ahead of time; they're stored locally and GPS keeps working without a network.
The maps are saved on the phone so they work in the mountains where there's no signal. It was one of the main features.

answers.why: False: GPS doesn't need mobile data, and Google Maps API tiles aren't fetched via GPS satellites.
answers.answer: Offline maps were easy because the phone downloads the map tiles directly from the GPS satellites, so you don't need internet at all, only GPS.
Offline functionality is very important for mobile applications in areas with poor connectivity. Many modern apps use caching strategies to provide a good user experience without network access.

items.question: Why did you preprocess the images before running OCR?

answers.why: Correct preprocessing steps with reasons and a measured effect.
answers.answer: Receipt photos are skewed, shadowed and low contrast, and Tesseract expects clean black text on white. So I convert to grayscale, use adaptive thresholding instead of a single global threshold because of the uneven lighting, deskew using the angle of the text lines, and remove small specks with a morphological open. On 60 test receipts, getting the total right went from about 55% to 84%.
Tesseract works best on clean binarised text, so grayscale, adaptive threshold and deskew made the totals much more readable.

answers.why: Wandering but contains the right reasons.
answers.answer: Honestly at first I just threw the raw photo at Tesseract and the output was garbage, like random symbols everywhere. Then I read about it and figured the lighting was the issue, shadows from the phone and stuff. So I did grayscale and thresholding, the adaptive one because one part of the receipt is darker, and also straightened the image. After that it actually started reading the totals properly most of the time.

answers.why: Core reasoning wrong: Tesseract does not work better on colour, and converting to RGB doesn't help.
answers.answer: Tesseract is trained on colour images, so I converted everything to full RGB and increased the saturation, which makes the text stand out more for the neural network.
OpenCV, Tesseract, FastAPI, grayscale, thresholding, deskew, OCR, preprocessing, regex.

items.question: How did you stop two hosts from seating the same party at the same time?

answers.why: Correct concurrency fix, explains the race, what the user sees.
answers.answer: That was a real bug: two hosts clicked seat on the same party within a second and it got two tables. The fix was doing the seat action in a transaction that locks the party row with select_for_update, then checks the status is still waiting before changing it. The second host's request waits for the lock, sees the party is already seated and gets a message instead. I reproduced it with two browser windows and a small sleep in the view.
Seating runs in a transaction with select_for_update on the party row and re-checks that it's still waiting, so the second click fails cleanly.

answers.why: UI-only mitigation; doesn't fix the race but is honest.
answers.answer: I disabled the seat button after one click and refresh the dashboard every few seconds. It mostly stopped it, though I think it could still happen if two people click at exactly the same time.

answers.why: False: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks rows, not the whole database.
answers.answer: I used SELECT FOR UPDATE, which locks the entire database while one host is seating, so nobody else can do anything until they're done. That's the safest way.
This is a classic race condition. Race conditions happen when multiple processes access shared data at the same time, and they are usually solved with locks, mutexes or transactions.

items.question: How did you deal with the API's rate limits in StockSense?

answers.why: Specific constraints, design decisions (dedupe, cache TTL, scheduling), trade-off.
answers.answer: The free tier only allowed a handful of requests a minute, and users kept adding the same tickers. So instead of polling per alert, I poll per unique ticker: the scheduler collects every distinct symbol with an active alert and spreads the requests across the minute to stay under the limit. Quotes go into Redis with a 60-second TTL, and every alert for that symbol is checked against the cached quote. The trade-off is alerts can be up to a minute late, which I said in the bot's help text.
Poll each distinct ticker once, spread the calls over the minute, and cache quotes in Redis for 60 seconds so all alerts reuse them.
I used Redis as a cache so we don't call the API too much. It helped with the limits.

answers.why: Wrong: rate limits are per API key, not per thread; parallel requests hit the limit faster.
answers.answer: I sent the requests in parallel with multithreading. The limit is counted per thread, so with ten threads I could make ten times more requests without being blocked.

answers.why: Implausible over-claim, unsupported by the resume.
answers.answer: I negotiated with Alpha Vantage and got unlimited enterprise access for free, so rate limits were never an issue for us.

items.question: Tell me about a production issue you helped fix during your internship at PayNest.

answers.why: Specific incident, correct root cause (max.poll.interval), fix, honest role.
answers.answer: Payment notifications were going out minutes late during peak hours. The consumer group kept rebalancing: one batch of events took longer than max.poll.interval.ms because each event made a slow call to the SMS provider, so Kafka assumed the consumer was dead and kicked it out, which paused everyone. My mentor led it, but I found the rebalance logs and wrote the fix with them: smaller max.poll.records and moving the SMS call to an async queue, so polling stays fast.
Consumers were exceeding max.poll.interval.ms because of slow SMS calls, causing rebalances; we cut the batch size and made the SMS call async.
There was an issue with delayed notifications. My mentor mostly fixed it, I helped check the logs and tested the fix in staging.

answers.why: False: Kafka doesn't lose messages because of consumer rebalancing; adding partitions doesn't make processing exactly-once.
answers.answer: Messages were getting lost because Kafka deletes them when consumers rebalance. We fixed it by adding more partitions, which makes Kafka deliver exactly once.
Production issues are a normal part of software engineering. The important thing is to stay calm, check the logs and metrics, find the root cause and communicate with the team.

items.question: Why did you use an LSTM rather than a plain CNN for SignSpeak?

answers.why: Correct reasoning about temporal signal, input representation, evidence from their experiment.
answers.answer: Most of the signs are defined by movement, not a single hand shape — 'thank you' and 'good' start from almost the same pose. A CNN on single frames only sees the pose. I feed the LSTM a sequence of 30 frames of MediaPipe landmarks, 21 points per hand, so it learns how the hands move over time, and since the inputs are coordinates instead of pixels the model stays small. A single-frame baseline I tried got around 70%; the LSTM got 91% on the held-out signer.
Signs depend on motion across frames, and an LSTM over landmark sequences captures that, while a CNN on single frames only sees one pose.

answers.why: Rambling but contains the correct reason and a comparison.
answers.answer: So we started with a CNN because that's what everyone uses for images right, and it was okay for static letters but really bad for words, like it kept confusing words that start the same way. Then my professor said words are about movement, so we switched to taking the landmark points from MediaPipe for a bunch of frames and putting that into an LSTM. It got way better, like 91 percent.

answers.why: Wrong reason: LSTMs are not generally faster or more accurate on images; the real reason (temporal motion) is missing.
answers.answer: LSTMs are faster than CNNs and always more accurate on images, because they have fewer layers. That's why every modern vision model uses LSTMs now.

items.question: Why did you choose InfluxDB instead of PostgreSQL for GreenGrid?

answers.why: Correct time-series reasoning, concrete volume, features used, honest trade-off.
answers.answer: It's almost all time-series writes: every plug sends a reading every 5 seconds, so ten plugs is about 170,000 points a day, and the dashboard only asks questions like average power per hour over the last week. InfluxDB is built for that — compressed time-ordered storage, retention policies so raw 5-second data is dropped after 30 days, and continuous downsampling into hourly averages. Postgres could do it with something like TimescaleDB, but I'd be building retention and rollups myself. The downside is user accounts don't belong in Influx, so those stay in a small SQLite file.
Lots of small timestamped writes and time-window queries; InfluxDB gives compression, retention policies and downsampling built in.
InfluxDB is better for sensor data and it was faster for our use case.

answers.why: False: InfluxDB is not a relational database with joins and foreign keys.
answers.answer: InfluxDB is a relational database like Postgres but faster, and it has better support for joins and foreign keys, which we needed for linking plugs to rooms.
A time-series database is a database optimized for storing data points indexed by time. They are commonly used for monitoring, IoT and financial data.
